A2.text:
Leyla is nineteen. Her grandfather, Akif, is the nard champion of the tea house on their street. Every year, there is a small tournament there. Only men play.

This year, Leyla wanted to play too. She practised nard on her phone every night for six months.

“Women never play here,” the old men said. But Akif said, “My granddaughter can play.”

Akif has many superstitions. He always sits on the same chair. Before every game, he touches the table and says, “Touch wood.” He also wears a blue charm against the evil eye.

In the first game, Leyla won. “Beginner's luck,” the men laughed. She won the second game, and the third. “It's a coincidence,” they said.

Leyla got to the final. Her opponent was her grandfather! The odds were against her, because Akif never loses.

Suddenly, Akif dropped the salt on the table. “That is a bad omen,” a man said. “Akif will lose.”

“Don't jinx me!” Akif laughed.

The game was long and difficult. Against all odds, Leyla won.

Everybody was quiet. Then Akif stood up and hugged her.

“It was not luck,” he said to the men. “She practised for six months. Luck is for people who don't practise.”

Then he smiled at Leyla. “Next year, touch wood, I will win.”

B1.text:
Leyla's grandfather Akif had been the nard champion of the tea house on Samed Vurgun Street for eleven years. The yearly tournament was an all-male affair, played under a vine with endless glasses of tea, and Leyla had watched it from the doorway since she was six.

This year, at nineteen, she signed up. For six months she had played every night on an app, studying the moves of the best online players.

The old men smiled politely. “It's not a place for girls,” one of them said. Akif just put his name next to hers on the board.

Her grandfather was a deeply superstitious man. He always sat in the same corner chair, never shook the dice with his left hand, and touched the wooden table before every game. “Touch wood,” he would say. A small blue charm against the evil eye hung from his keys.

Leyla won her first match easily. “Beginner's luck,” someone said. She won the second. “Coincidence.” By the time she reached the semi-final, nobody was laughing any more.

The final was Leyla against Akif. Everybody agreed the odds were impossible: he had not lost a game there in three years. Just before they started, Akif knocked over the salt. A murmur went round the tables. “A bad omen,” whispered his old friend Rauf.

“Don't jinx me, you fool,” Akif said, grinning.

They played for nearly an hour. It wasn't a gamble — every move Leyla made was a calculation. And against all odds, she won by a single piece.

For a moment there was total silence. Then Akif stood up and kissed her forehead.

“Some of you will call it fate,” he told the room. “I call it six months of practice while you were all asleep.”

He sat back down and started setting up the board again. “Now, one more. Touch wood, this time I'll be ready.”

B2.text:
For eleven consecutive years, the nard tournament at the tea house on Samed Vurgun Street had ended the same way: with Leyla's grandfather Akif sweeping the pieces into their box and accepting the congratulations of men who had long since stopped expecting to beat him. It was an exclusively male institution, conducted beneath a sagging vine to the clatter of dice and the endless refilling of pear-shaped glasses, and Leyla had observed it from the doorway since she was old enough to walk.

At nineteen, she put her name on the board. She had spent the previous six months playing nightly on an app, dissecting the strategies of players from Istanbul to Tehran.

The regulars received the news with exaggerated courtesy. “Not really a place for young ladies,” one remarked. Akif said nothing; he simply wrote his own name beneath hers.

Her grandfather's superstitions were the stuff of family legend. He occupied the same corner chair without exception, refused to shake the dice left-handed and rapped his knuckles on the wooden table before each game. “Touch wood,” he would mutter. Dangling from his keys was a blue glass charm to deflect the evil eye.

Leyla dispatched her first opponent briskly. “Beginner's luck,” someone concluded. She won again. “Pure coincidence.” By the semi-final, the commentary had stopped altogether.

The final, inevitably, was granddaughter against grandfather, and the odds were considered absurd — Akif had not dropped a single game on those premises in three years. As they sat down, his sleeve caught the salt cellar and sent it skidding across the table. A ripple went through the room. “That's an omen,” breathed his oldest friend Rauf.

“Don't jinx me, you old crow,” Akif replied cheerfully.

The match lasted almost an hour. Nothing about it resembled a gamble: every move Leyla made had been rehearsed a thousand times on a glowing screen at two in the morning. And against all odds, she took the game by a single piece.

The silence was absolute. Then Akif rose, cupped her face in his hands and kissed her forehead.

“Some of you will say it was fate,” he announced. “I'd say it was six months of discipline while the rest of you slept.”

Then he sat down and began laying out the pieces again. “Another,” he said. “Touch wood, this time I'll be paying attention.”
